Adopting weft in an existing report

Source: vignettes/adopting.Rmd
adopting.Rmd

This article is for an author with a long report that already renders: a statistics report in R Markdown or Quarto, with its own helpers, its own house style and many numbers typed into the prose. After it you will know what to turn on first, what the first renders will report, and how to decide how hard each kind of check should fail.

None of the code in this article is run when the article is built.

The order to work in

Adopt weft in small steps, and commit after each one. Each step leaves a report that renders.

  1. Set up, change nothing else. Run weft::use_weft() (see vignette("setup", package = "weft")). Render. A document with no constructs renders as it did: weft adds the ledger and its checks of the rendered output, and prints the same text.
  2. Read the first render’s report, below, and fix what it finds. Then commit the source with _weft/ledger/. The gate passes the first commit by design: it refuses only what HEAD did not hold.
  3. Set the house style in _weft.yml, so that values print as the report already prints them.
  4. Convert one chapter: typed numbers to values, helpers to classes, direction words to spans, stopifnot() to claim().
  5. Collect chunk claims, so that one render lists every failure.
  6. Add severity patterns for the warnings your models raise.
  7. Before release, turn draft mode off and run verify().

What the first renders report

The first render of an existing report can report three kinds of thing.

  • The rendered-output check. A cross-reference Quarto could not resolve, which it printed as “?@sec-…” and only warned about in its log, now fails the render. An “NA” in the prose is a warned check. A fence Pandoc did not read fails. These were in the output before; weft now says so. See vignette("gate", package = "weft").
  • Conditions. The condition log records every warning and message a chunk raised, warning: false or not. A warning or message fails nothing unless it matches a severity pattern, but changes() lists each new one.
  • Construct errors, once you start writing constructs: a misspelt class, two classes from one group. They stop the render at once and name the line.

lints() reports typed numbers, but the gate tolerates every one already committed. The count of tolerated findings that verify() prints is how far adoption has come.

A project that upgrades weft rather than adopting it sees one more thing once: the first render after the upgrade lists every table of each ledger as added. Commit the ledgers and it is gone.

The house style

Most reports have a style weft can reproduce with settings. A typical _weft.yml for a statistics report:

serial_comma: true        # "A, B, and C"
count_threshold: 11       # .count spells one to ten, digits from 11
numeral_years: true       # a year in prose is not a typed number
label_words: [Site, Plot, Model]
anchor_calls: [fig_with_label]
p_digits: 3               # "p = 0.046", "p < 0.001", "p = 0.120"
p_label: "*p*"            # an italic p
ci_short: true            # "2.1 (1.3 to 2.9)"
chunk_claims: collect     # see below

numeral_years and label_words cut the numeral lint’s findings to the numbers that are quantities. label_seed() proposes label words from the prose. anchor_calls names your own helpers that create a figure or table label, so the cross-reference lints know those anchors exist (see vignette("lints", package = "weft")).

A rule no class covers goes in a project formatter. A report that prints whole percentages from 10% up and two significant figures below:

formatters:
  .pctrule:
    function: pct_rule
    stage: number
pct_rule <- function(x) {
  ifelse(abs(x) >= 0.1, weft::fmt_pct(x, digits = 0), weft::fmt_pct(x, sigfig = 2))
}

`r share`{.pctrule} then prints “23%” for 0.234 and “4.6%” for 0.0456.

Helpers to classes

A report’s own formatting helpers map onto classes. Replace each call in the prose, and keep the helper only where code still needs it:

In the report With weft
`r scales::percent(x)`, `r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100 * x)` `r x`{.pct}
`r format(x, big.mark = ',')` `r x`{.num}
`r nice_p(p)` `r p`{.p}
`r paste0(ifelse(d > 0, '+', ''), round(d, 1))` `r d`{.num .plus}
`r paste(est, ' (', lo, '–', hi, ')')` `r ci(est, lo, hi)`
`r paste(x, collapse = ', ')` `r x`{.and}
a word chosen with ifelse(d > 0, "rose", "fell") [rose \| fell \| did not change]{sign="d"}
stopifnot(n >= 10) before a sentence n <- claim(n, . >= 10) where n is made

The last two are the ones that matter most. A direction word chosen by a span cannot disagree with its number, and a claim fails the render with the sentence quoted, where stopifnot() stopped with a bare message. See vignette("wording", package = "weft").

Text that a chunk prints with results: asis, such as a list of questions or one sentence per site, is converted with weft_str() or with named values (see “Text a chunk prints” in vignette("named-values", package = "weft")).

Reads weft can and cannot follow

The ledger records each target a document reads, so that changes() and verify() can say when a value was not re-rendered. A report that reads its store through a helper of its own is followed when the helper passes one of its arguments as the name:

read_t <- function(name, store = here::here("_targets")) {
  targets::tar_read_raw(name, store = store)
}
read_t("fit_main")      # recorded: target fit_main, from the default store

A store that is not a literal is evaluated at the end of the knit, so the default above resolves. These are not followed:

read_shared <- function(id) targets::tar_read_raw(paste0("shared_", id))
#   the helper builds the name, so no call names a target
read_local <- function(name) {
  s <- file.path(root, "_targets")
  targets::tar_read_raw(name, store = s)
}
#   the store is a local of the helper: the read is recorded under the
#   default store, with a warning that names it
source(here::here("R", "helpers.R"))
#   only a literal path is recorded as a file the document read

Where a read matters to the report, pass the name and the store as arguments, or read the target by its literal name. See vignette("targets", package = "weft").

Activation: .Rprofile or front matter

use_setup() activates weft through the project’s .Rprofile in a Quarto project, and through each document’s front matter elsewhere.

  • Choose the .Rprofile for a book or website: every chapter is covered, including one added later. The file keeps your own ~/.Rprofile and renv’s activation.
  • Choose front matter for documents that travel on their own, or where a project .Rprofile would be a surprise to others.

A collaborator without weft can still start R in the project. Their renders print each span as plain text, so render releases where weft is installed.

Coding agents

use_agent_docs() writes the rules a coding agent should follow into AGENTS.md and a skill. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md: add the line @AGENTS.md to CLAUDE.md. See vignette("agents", package = "weft").

Choosing how hard a check fails

weft has three strengths for a check, and a report needs all three.

A failing check stops the render, or fails it at the end, with the sentence quoted. Use it when the sentence is false if the check fails: “most sites rose” needs n_up > n_sites / 2.

n_up <- claim(sum(trend$up), . > n_sites / 2)

A warned check, level = "warn", is listed at the end of the render and never fails it. Use it for a condition worth a look that does not make any sentence false, such as a sample smaller than the method prefers:

n_obs <- claim(nrow(d), . >= 30, level = "warn")

Do not weaken a failing check to a warned one to get a render through. The commit gate treats them differently: a warned check that remains does not cover a failing one that was removed.

Settings set the strength of weft’s own checks, each fail, warn or off:

Setting Default Checks
output_refs fail references Quarto could not resolve
output_missing warn NA, NaN or Inf printed in the prose
output_markup fail markup Pandoc did not read

Three more settings move a check between levels: bare_missing: false turns off the warning on a bare value that prints NA; sentence_start_fail: true fails a numeral at the start of a sentence; chunk_claims: collect keeps the knit going after a failing claim in a chunk and fails the render at the end. A lint is tolerated while old findings remain, and fails on any finding once it is listed in strict.

Draft mode is not a strength. It reports every failure and fails nothing, for a chapter half written; verify() refuses to run in it.

Model-convergence warnings

A model that did not converge usually warns and returns estimates anyway, and the report prints them. The severity list in _weft.yml turns a warning or message that matches one of its patterns into a failure. weft ships two patterns: a singular fit and a non-positive-definite Hessian. For lme4 and glmmTMB add:

severity:
  - "failed to converge"
  - "Model failed to converge with max\\|grad\\|"
  - "false convergence"

The patterns are regular expressions, so the bars in max|grad| are escaped. lme4 prints “failed to converge” and “Model failed to converge with max|grad| = …”; glmmTMB prints “false convergence” and “non-positive-definite Hessian matrix”, the second of which the shipped pattern already covers. A project’s patterns add to the shipped ones.

A warning raised inside a targets pipeline is matched too, when the document reads that target: the condition log takes the warnings that targets::tar_meta() holds for it. A message raised there is not.
